sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Tūmatauenga** (*tumatauenga*) — The Face of Battle — belongs to the Polynesian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "War, Humanity, Strength". The name means "'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind"[^1].

Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god attacked, and who then subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Tūmatauenga** and serves its temple at [tūmatauenga.com](https://xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *tumatauenga* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.
The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, Lyon and Blair, 1891.
George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, Brett, Auckland, 1855.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Tūmatauenga** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind"[^1].

The ASCII form *tumatauenga* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Tūmatauenga** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **m** → **m** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **g** → **g** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **tūmatauenga.com** (xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/tuː.ma.taʊ.ˈe.ŋa/** — Māori.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: TOO-mah-tow-ENG-ah, long ū on the first syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Māori** — Tūmatauenga
- **Hawaiian twin** — Kū
- **NZ Army** — Ngāti Tūmatauenga
- **Owned form** — Tūmatauenga

Tūmatauenga is pronounced with the long ū of the first syllable — the macron the restoration keeps — and the name means "Tū of the angry face": tū (to stand, and the god's name) plus mata (face) plus anga (the -ing of appearance). He is the Māori war-god, and his name is a face set for war.

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual polynesian names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Tūmatauenga** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Te reo Māori writes him with the macron as the vowel-length it is: Tūmatauenga. The oral text is the truer scripture — the whakataukī "Ka mate kāinga tahi, ka ora kāinga rua" and the karakia of war and planting carry his name in the living language, and the New Zealand Army's Māori name, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, writes it into the state itself.

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god attacked, and who then subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.[^1]

### The Mere

The flat greenstone club of the chief — the weapon that is also a badge of rank and a gift of state.

### The Angry Face

His name: the war-face (pūkana) that the haka still performs with widened eyes and out-thrust tongue.

### The Nets and Hooks

He snared his brother Tangaroa's fish: the arts of fishing, won by war and given to man.

### The Pa

The fortified hill-settlement — his architecture, crowning New Zealand's ridgelines by the thousand.

sources.citation: The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, Lyon and Blair, 1891.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Tūmatauenga concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The taiaha** — The long staff-weapon of chiefly combat — spear and club in one lineage
- **The haka** — The war-dance: the body made into the angry face of the god
- **The feather cloak** — The kahu huruhuru of the war-chief — honour worn on the shoulders

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Tūmatauenga's cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children.[^1]

### The Sons of Rangi and Papa (The Separation)

In the beginning the Sky Father (Ranginui) and the Earth Mother (Papatūānuku) lay locked together, and their sons lived crushed in darkness between them. Tūmatauenga, fiercest of the brothers, urged that the parents be killed; the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed — they would be forced apart. Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tāne each tried and failed to push them; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and war came with it.[^2]

### The One Who Stood (The Storm)

Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation, and now he attacked his brothers in revenge: Tangaroa fled to the sea, the gods of food hid in the earth and the forest — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast against the storm, unbowed on the open plain. When the tempest spent itself, the war-god turned on his fleeing brothers: he made nets and took Tangaroa's fish, snared Tāne's birds, and dug up Rongo's and Haumia's crops. His standing made humanity heir to every domain.

### The Arts of War and Peace (The Inheritance)

By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their realms noa — common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: net and hook for the sea, snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden. The karakia of planting, fishing, and war all carry his name; the Māori tradition is explicit that the fierce god is also the culture-bringer. His children — humanity, in the southern traditions — inherited both the standing and the storm.

sources.citation: The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary, Lyon and Blair, 1891.
George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, Brett, Auckland, 1855.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the feathered helmets and the luakini temples — Tahitian Tū, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion. In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and their tohunga; the 19th-century Māori military genius (the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars) applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, "the tribe of the war-god."[^1]

Within the Polynesian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[kanaloa|Kānāloa]], [[papatuanuku|Papatūānuku]], [[tane|Tāne]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[anat|ꜥAnat]], and [[ares|Árēs]].

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The haka — performed by the All Blacks before every match and by the army at every farewell — is his face in modern life: the widened eyes and out-thrust tongue are the literal mata anga of his name. Ngāti Tūmatauenga, the army's Māori designation, makes him the only ancient god officially patron of a modern state's armed forces. His cycle — the standing against the storm, the conquest that feeds the people — remains the charter myth of Māori resilience, quoted in land-march speeches and waiata alike.[^1]

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: New Zealand's ridgelines keep his monuments: thousands of pa — terraced, ditched, and palisaded hill-forts — from the classic period, with sites like Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) among the largest earthworks of the Pacific. The greenstone mere and the carved taiaha of the museum collections (Te Papa's among them) are his regalia; the Auckland War Memorial Museum — itself a cenotaph to the fallen — houses the war-canoes and the martial taonga of his people. The kumara storage-pits beside every pa tie his war-and-garden cycle into the ground itself.[^1]

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.

sections.label: Oral Narratives
sections.body:
The war-god's names are a catalogue of fierceness, kept in the karakia.

- **Tū-te-awheawhe** — 'Tū of the angry visage'; the full expansion of his name.
- **Tū-whakaheke-tangata** — 'Tū who causes man to descend'; the war-god as man's undoing.
- **Tū-kai-taua** — 'Tū who feasts on war-parties'; the battle-title.
- **Tū-matauenga** — 'Tū of the angry face'; the standing form.
- **Kū** — his Hawaiian name, the war-god of the feathered helmets, the same god across the ocean.

sources.citation: Grey, Polynesian Mythology (Tū cycle); Tregear, Maori Dictionary.

sections.label: Ethnographic Sources
sections.body: The ethnographic file begins with **George Grey's Polynesian Mythology** (1855), which took the separation and the storm from Māori tohunga directly and remains the cycle's standard text; **Tregear's** Maori-Polynesian comparative dictionary documents the Tū/Kū name-field across the islands; **Elsdon Best's** Māori religion studies preserve the war-karakia and the pa rites; and **Handy's** Polynesian Religion sets him beside Hawaiian Kū. The New Zealand Army's adoption of his name (Ngāti Tūmatauenga) is itself now cited as the ethnography's latest chapter.

sources.citation: Grey, Polynesian Mythology; Best, Māori Religion; Handy, Polynesian Religion.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Tūmatauenga is the god of standing your ground — and of what standing costs. He alone faced the storm, and so he alone could feed the people; but the myth hides nothing: his fierceness proposed killing the parents, and his victories are his brothers' defeats. He asks the hardest question of every defender: what are you standing against — and what, when you have won, will your strength feed?[^1]

sources.citation: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, John Murray, London; New Zealand Electronic Text Centre, 1855.
